passage: Prize-day rehearsal was in ten minutes, and the hall was full of drums and chairs scraping. Parul Ma'am snapped, "Vasudha, stop talking! You are ruining this," though it was the boy behind her who had been talking. Vasudha's ears burned. She had always thought Parul Ma'am was the fairest teacher. She said nothing through the whole practice. Afterwards, when the hall emptied, Vasudha walked up and said, "Ma'am, I felt bad when you said it was me. It was not." Parul Ma'am paused, then said, "I was rushed and I got it wrong. I am sorry."

qa.q: How much time was left before the prize-day rehearsal in the passage?
qa.a: There were ten minutes left before the rehearsal.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when Parul Ma'am blamed her?
qa.a: She was shocked and hurt, since her ears burned and she had thought Parul Ma'am was the fairest teacher.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do well by waiting until the hall emptied?
qa.a: She spoke politely and privately about how she felt, which gave the teacher a chance to admit the mistake without being embarrassed. 🙂

qa.q: How might Parul Ma'am have seen the situation while rushing?
qa.a: She was under time pressure in a noisy hall and probably reacted without looking carefully, then recognised her error when Vasudha spoke up.

grounding: A child is shocked when her favourite teacher is unfair, then politely tells her how she felt without cutting her off.

passage:
Tuesday. Mrs Pillai was Lavanya's favourite teacher. So when Harish whispered a joke and Mrs Pillai turned and said, 'Lavanya, outside. I expected better,' Lavanya was too shocked to speak. She stood in the corridor, cheeks burning. She hadn't said a word.
Wednesday. Lavanya didn't put her hand up once. At home she told Amma she was never speaking to Mrs Pillai again. Amma said, 'That's one choice. Or you could tell her.'
Thursday. After class, Lavanya waited by the desk, heart thumping. 'Ma'am, on Tuesday it wasn't me talking. It felt really unfair.' Mrs Pillai looked surprised, then sorry. 'Thank you for telling me, Lavanya. I got that wrong.' Lavanya put her hand up in the very next lesson.

qa.q: What did Mrs Pillai say to Lavanya on Tuesday?
What was Lavanya feeling in the corridor?
qa.a: Shocked and hurt; her cheeks burned because her favourite teacher had blamed her unfairly.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than never speaking to Mrs Pillai again?
qa.a: Politely telling her after class that it wasn't her and that it felt unfair.

qa.q: How did Mrs Pillai respond when Lavanya spoke up?
qa.a: She was surprised, then sorry; she thanked Lavanya and admitted she got it wrong.

grounding: Over three days a girl is shocked when her favourite teacher is unfair, then politely tells her how it felt.

passage: 'Ira, you're sulking because Miss said something unfair? Listen to your Salma Nani. When I was eleven, I adored our Urdu teacher, Begum Sahiba. She wrote poems on the board in beautiful curls. One day she tore up my essay in front of everyone, saying I had copied it from my sister. I hadn't. I wrote it myself, by lamplight, over three nights. I felt as if the ground had cracked. I wanted never to read her poems again. My father said, "Go and tell her, politely." So I did, the next week, with the rough pages in my hand. She read them, and her face changed. She said sorry in front of the class. She was only a person, beta. People get things wrong.'

qa.q: What did young Salma bring to show the teacher?
qa.a: The rough pages of her essay.

qa.q: How did young Salma feel when her essay was torn up?
qa.a: Shocked and deeply hurt, as if the ground had cracked, because she had written it herself.

qa.q: What choice in the story mended things?
qa.a: Politely showing the teacher the rough pages instead of cutting her off forever.

qa.q: How might Begum Sahiba have felt reading the rough pages?
qa.a: Surprised and sorry; her face changed and she apologised in front of the class.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a favourite teacher being unfair, and how politely telling her mended things.
